articleTitle: Highlights of Antenna Innovations (1974–2024): New developments over recent decades
abstract: This overview article provides examples of new antenna development across the past 50 years. Among others, the article highlights planar and conformal antennas, small antennas, fractals, apertures/arrays, Vivaldis and tightly coupled dipole arrays (TCDAs), active antennas, metamaterial apertures, textured materials antennas, magneto-piezoelectric antennas, non-Foster impedance matching, electromagnetic bandgap (EBG) antennas, automotive antennas, handset antennas, multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) antennas, millimeter-wave (mmWave) antennas, terahertz antennas, medical application antennas and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs), and reflector antennas.

articleTitle: Design of a Large-Scale Efficient and Low-Cost High-Frequency Spectrum Monitoring Network: The case of Greece
abstract: The development of a large-scale widespread spectrum monitoring network (SMN) is essential for spectrum management and interference identification at a national level. The financial outlay involved in setting up such a system is considerable, encompassing the acquisition of requisite equipment and installation infrastructure. However, the expenses can be significantly curtailed by leveraging the existing infrastructure of other service providers, such as mobile network operators (MNOs), via collocation. Nevertheless, this strategy requires the selection of suitable sites among the available ones to develop an SMN that is both efficient and cost-effective. Toward this end, this article presents the methodological framework for designing a nationwide SMN by collocating with existing MNOs’ infrastructure. The proposed approach is evaluated using computer simulations in the context of the spectrum monitoring requirements in Greece. Specifically, the network’s performance is assessed according to International Telecommunication Union (ITU) guidelines and the spectrum limitations of Greece’s national regulatory authority (NRA). The results demonstrate that a network based on time difference of arrival (TDoA) with 160 sensors can adequately cover the entire region, including the mainland, islands, and surrounding seas. Adding angle-of-arrival (AoA) capabilities to 30 out of 160 sites enables the hybrid geolocation technology and improves the geolocation ability and accuracy of the SMN network noticeably.

articleTitle: Novel Hybrid Particle Swarm and Brainstorm Optimization: Electromagnetic applications with enhanced performance
abstract: In this paper, we introduce and investigate a hybridization algorithm based on particle swarm optimization (PSO) and brain storm optimization (BSO). The hybrid BSO-PSO (HBPSO) technique adopts particle swarm optimization that is initialized by brain storm optimization within the starting iterations. Performance of the HBPSO is significantly enhanced comparing to single BSO or PSO, when applying to high-dimensional optimization problems with local minima. The hybrid procedure is validated by showing appropriate convergence curves when applying to five benchmark functions. Guidelines regarding the selection of inertial factor and switching iteration is investigated and presented accordingly. The proposed HBPSO is then validated using practical optimization tasks. It is demonstrated that HBPSO could outperform single PSO or BSO techniques in addressing representative antenna-related problems, including patch antenna circuit model extraction, conformal antenna array synthesis and full-wave antenna design problems.

articleTitle: Review on Wearable Antennas: Part 2: Recent advances and applications
abstract: Wearable antennas assume a critical role in wearable devices and systems, facilitating real-time remote data and energy transmission wirelessly. Unlike their conventional rigid counterparts, wearable antennas impose more stringent criteria. In addition to necessitating flexibility and conformity to the human body, wearable antennas demand compactness to fit in miniature wearable devices while maintaining satisfied radiation performance. Furthermore, these antennas are expected to possess multi-band or wideband operational capabilities to suit diverse application scenarios and Industrial, Scientific, and Medical (ISM) bands. Additionally, preference is given to antennas that are reconfigurable, permitting tunability of frequency, radiation pattern, and polarization. Such adaptability renders the antenna suitable for both on-body and free-space operations, or scenarios necessitating modifications to the functionality of wearable devices without necessitating alterations to other components. In pursuit of these objectives, diverse wearable antenna prototypes have recently been developed. This comprehensive review systematically presents recent advancements in miniature, multi-band and wideband, and reconfigurable wearable antennas, examining their applications in health monitoring, tracking, and energy harvesting, providing valuable insights for the development of wearable antennas and systems.

articleTitle: Near-Field Technologies for Multifunction Wireless Connectivity: Recent principles and applications
abstract: Antenna and array technologies have been in constant evolution since more than one-hundred years for various purposed wireless connectivity among devices and/or systems distantly by radiating electromagnetic waves, usually operating in a far-field manner. With the proliferation of the Internet of Things (IoT) that started more than two decades ago, wireless devices are often required to transfer, share, read, and store their information over a short distance in a secure and efficient way, which may not fall into the category of far-field applications. However, the conventional theories and techniques for far-field applications cannot generally be applied directly for the development of a short-range communication because the nature of electromagnetic fields in the near-field region is quite different from that in the far-field region. Therefore, the near-field theories were developed for accurately describing the phenomenon of waves in antenna near-field region then yield novel and practical applications. This article encompasses the recent developed principles and applications of near-field technique for multifunction wireless connectivity including near-field coupling, imaging, and signal processing.

articleTitle: Prior-Knowledge Incorporated Forward and Reverse Neural Network Modeling for Estimating Performance Parameters of Band-Notched UWB MIMO Antennas: Smart estimation strategies
abstract: Design and analysis of MIMO antennas using electromagnetic (EM) simulator is a computationally expensive process. In this case, artificial neural network (ANN) can be effectively used to obtain a surrogate model. The accuracy and requirement of large data samples can be improved by incorporating prior knowledge into the ANN model. Hence in this article, a prior knowledge input (PKI) method-based ANN model has been presented for modeling MIMO antennas. Two UWB MIMO antenna designs with band notch characteristics have been proposed. The MIMO antenna designed using FR4 substrate has four ports and rejects two interfering bands X-band Downlink (6.3-7.6 GHz) and Uplink (8.05-8.7 GHz). The analysis and synthesis of the MIMO antennas are achieved using PKI forward and reverse modeling method. The performance of the PKI model is found to outperform the standard ANN model in terms of the error variation. Also, prototypes of both the MIMO antennas are fabricated and characterized. The simulated, computed and measured counterparts are found to be in good agreement with each other.

articleTitle: Long-Distance Radio Communication 100 Years Ago: The Alexanderson System at Radio Central [Historically Speaking]
abstract: About one hundred years ago, the Radio Corporation of America (RCA) set out to build a complex called Radio Central at Rocky Point, Long Island, NY that was supposed to be the “last word” in long-distance, trans-oceanic radio communication. The facility for transmission was based on a system, remarkable for the time, developed at the General Electric Company (GE), principally by Ernst F. W. Alexanderson, and therefore often referred to as the Alexanderson System for Radio Communication. The main objective for this article is to provide the reader with a simple description of the basic physics, principally the electromagnets, underpinning a few of the key components of this historically important system. In addition, the circumstances that made RCA decide to build this facility as well as those that caused RCA to eventually limit its development are discussed.

articleTitle: Review of Wearable Antennas: Part 1: Materials, fabrication, and radiation characteristics
abstract: Wearable antennas have raised much interest in recent years, due to their capacity for facilitating wireless sensing and communication in a lightweight, flexible, portable, and cost-effective manner. This comprehensive review explores the materials, fabrication techniques, and characteristics of recent wearable antennas. The materials and fabrication processes of wearable antennas assume critical significance, as wearable antennas are expected to offer flexibility and comfort during wear while simultaneously maintaining optimal radiation efficiency. Moreover, beyond conventional antenna characteristics, such as gain, directivity, and efficiency, the design of wearable antennas necessitates consideration of additional factors. These factors include the impact of the human body and its deformations on antenna performance as well as safety considerations about antenna radiation effects on the human body. By comprehensively discussing antenna materials, fabrication techniques, and characteristics, this article aims to provide an overview of recent wearable antennas, shedding light on their potential applications on wearable systems and the health-care Internet of Things (IoT).

articleTitle: Quantum Computing for Antennas and Propagation Problems: A gentle introduction.
abstract: Quantum computing is a cutting-edge paradigm in data processing that uses the principles of quantum mechanics to perform calculations. It has promising applications in various fields of engineering, including applied electromagnetism. Like any emerging technology, quantum computing has advantages and limitations that require in-depth understanding to make effective use in real-world engineering applications. This article aims to provide a simple and intuitive introduction to the fundamental principles of quantum computing, delving into the strengths and limitations inherent to this innovative technology and suggesting some applications of interest in the antennas and propagation community.

articleTitle: Quantum Annealing for Electromagnetic Engineers—Part II: Examples of electromagnetic problems solved by quantum annealing
abstract: It is well known that electromagnetic computations are computationally demanding. Interestingly, many such problems can be recast to be solved by quantum annealing. Quantum annealing, a kind of quantum computer, utilizes quantum tunneling for state transitions, which enables one to find the global minimum in a complex energy landscape. Part I of this article explains quantum annealing for the classical electromagnetic community, assuming little knowledge of quantum theory. Both the basic principle and recent developments to extend its applications, such as hybrid quantum–classical annealing, are reviewed. Part II presents various examples of electromagnetic problems that can be solved by quantum annealing. Those are 1) optimization of a reconfigurable directional metasurface, 2) finding current distribution in an arbitrary wire antenna, 3) finding charge and field distributions in a static condition, and 4) optimization of source excitation to focus fields in hyperthermia. Finally, the performance of quantum annealer is compared with classical solvers to deduce the type of application in which a quantum annealer of current technologies can be preferred in practice.

articleTitle: Pluses and Minuses: Cognizance of an Empiricist. [Young Professionals]
abstract: Life is a race, and you have to run—no choice! So, it’s better to be willingly a marathoner rather than a forced dragger. My lifelong marathon began in a beautiful village in Jammu and Kashmir, a valley surrounded by the majestic mountains of Pir Panjal, a true heaven on Earth (Figure 1)! My father Khalil Ur-Rehman, a true fighter and my inspiration, became an orphan at the age of 12. Being the eldest in a family of seven siblings with a good level of land ownership, he had to leave the school to earn bread. Despite self-educating himself through all the hardship to keep up with the long family legacy of prominent Islamic scholars, he was truly resentful of not being formally educated in a school. This made him very careful and focused on the education of his four children, resulting in three doctors and one engineer. Life in the mountains of developing nations is difficult with limited resources and infrastructure. However, people truly value education and make efforts to gain it, in its literal meanings. My eldest brother, Habib, used to travel 5 mi to reach his primary school. Although the situation is much better with many more schools now, the struggle is still on. Nevertheless, people in the northern mountainous region have the highest learning rate in the region.

articleTitle: A Journey During Six Years of the “Women in Engineering” Column [Women in Engineering]
abstract: I wrote my first contribution to the “Women in Engineering (WIE)” column for IEEE Antennas and Propagation Magazine (APM) in December 2018 to start a new adventure and try to find scientists and researchers interested in contributing. Now, for six years I have been responsible for the WiE column, and I sincerely thank my colleague and friend Claire Migliaccio for inviting me again to write a contribution: Claire will be the new WIE column appointed associate editor starting in 2025.
